headline: Nyatt Point after dark: bass on bunker while scup and fluke carry the daylight shift
subhead: The bay's gone warm and lazy in the sun, so the stripers punched out for the night crew — everything else is picking up the slack.
body_markdown:
Ran into Sal down at the Fields Point pier Tuesday morning, coffee in one hand, a rod he hadn't even rigged yet in the other, just standing there watching the water move. He said it plain: "Bay's warm, Vinny. Warm and slow." And he wasn't wrong. You can feel it in the air off the river now — that thick, still July heat that sits on the water and doesn't leave with the tide. Buckeye Brook's herring run is long done, the alewives pushed through back in April and May, and the bass that rode that bait into the upper bay have scattered out and gone quiet during the day. What's left is a nighttime program, and if you're not willing to fish dark or first light, you're leaving fish on the table.

I've been working the bridge structure — Mount Hope, the Jamestown side, pilings down by Conimicut — after 9 PM with success that daylight just isn't giving up right now. Eels are still the call, six to nine inches, drifted or slow-swum right along the current break where the light from the bridge deck cuts the shadow line. Bass are sitting right on that edge waiting for bait to get confused by the light, and they'll eat an eel fished slow better than anything with a hook in it right now. Bunker pods have been showing in the upper bay too, rolling off Nyatt Point and down toward Conimicut Light on the last of the ebb, and where you find bunker stacked tight, there are bass underneath them even in this heat — they just won't touch it till the sun's off the water. Snag-and-drop with a circle hook has worked for guys willing to sit on those pods till dusk.

Daytime, it's fluke and scup carrying the report, and honestly they're carrying it well. Fluke have been steady in the west passage off Rocky Point and down around the Hope Island flats, four to twelve feet of water, drifting the moving tide with a white or pink Gulp Swimming Mullet on a bucktail, three-quarter ounce when the current's got some push, half ounce when it slacks off. Nothing giant — most going 16 to 19 inches — but there's enough of them stacked on that softer bottom to make an afternoon worth it, especially with the neap tide we just rolled into softening the current everywhere in the bay. Weaker moving water means longer, more comfortable drift windows instead of getting blown through the zone in ten minutes flat.

Scup are doing exactly what scup do in late July — piled up on every rocky ledge and rubble pile from Prudence Island down to the Colt State Park side, and around the rocks off Rocky Point itself. Small hooks, sandworms or squid strips, right on bottom, and you can load a bucket in an hour if you find the right piece of structure on the last two hours of the incoming. It's not glamorous fishing but it's about as close to a sure thing as this bay's got right now, and it's good eating besides.

Greenwich Bay's been the other bright spot — weakfish have started showing again on the calm, warm evenings, right where we figured they'd come back once the water settled. We called that one last week, said the weakfish bite would rebuild on quiet nights, and that's exactly what's happened along the edges of the eelgrass flats there, small soft plastics on light jigheads worked slow just after dark. Nothing to brag about in numbers yet, but the pattern is real and it's building.

There's also been squid pushing into the bay, which is a good sign even if nobody's specifically targeting them — it means there's forage stacking up, and that's usually the thing that gets predators moving with more confidence once the heat breaks a little. I don't expect a big thermal shift in the next several days, so I'm not calling for anything to change dramatically. What I am saying is this warm-water pattern isn't going anywhere soon, so plan around it instead of fighting it.

If I've got one night this week, I'm fishing the last two hours of dusk into full dark off the Mount Hope Bridge rocks with eels, betting the bass show up once the light goes flat. If that doesn't produce, Plan B is first light at Rocky Point ledges for scup and a fluke drift on the way back in. Keep an eye on the bunker — if those pods hold in the upper bay through the week, the night bite off Conimicut and Nyatt should only get better as more bass slide up under them. Watch the neap tide too — slower water this week means longer bites, not shorter ones, so there's no reason to rush your drift.
